newsitem.title: USA: Clinton begins Act Two with second-term inaugural.
newsitem.headline: Clinton begins Act Two with second-term inaugural.

text.p: Bill Clinton began Act Two of a sometimes turbulent presidency on Monday, riding a sudden swell of popular esteem and optimism as he prepared to take his oath as the last U.S. president of the 20th century.

Clinton, 50, buffeted by controversies and missteps early in his first term and looking like a one-term dud two years ago, took the triumphal limousine ride reserved for White House winners for the traditional open-air swearing-in ceremony on Capitol Hill at about noon EST (1700 GMT)
Clinton, accompanied by wife Hillary and teenaged daughter Chelsea, was to take his oath for a second four-year term from Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist.

Thousands of dignitaries and invited guests, bundled up against the midwinter cold on a dry but cloudy day, gathered for the ceremony outside Congress on a bluff with a panoramic view across a red-white-and-blue bedecked Washington past the White House to the Potomac River.

Clinton dropped hints all weekend that his inaugural address, always an occasion for broad inspirational themes, would include calls to national and political harmony to address the urgent tasks of moving into the new millennium after years of brutal partisan warfare between Democratic White House and Republican Congress.
He described it in one interview, with the Washington Post, as a desire to "flush the poison out of the atmosphere."
There was plenty of need for that.

The U.S. capital in effect was only taking a day off from the wrenching procedure of punishing Republican House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich for ethics violations -- that will resume on Tuesday with a House vote -- and decking itself out for now in flags, bunting and inaugural finery instead of dirty linen.
And the personal controversy spotlight will swing back to Clinton as soon as it leaves Gingrich.

A continuing investigation of the Whitewater Arkansas financial affair and a new one into Democratic presidential campaign fund-raising practices face him as well as an attempt by a former Arkansas state employee to sue him for alleged sexual harassment in 1991 when he was Arkansas governor.

But those were headaches for another day. This one belonged to William Jefferson Clinton, reaffirmed as 42nd president of the United States as well as the 18th and last to hold that office in this century.

He was basking in several opinion polls putting his job approval rating as high as it has ever been since he took office four years ago -- around 60 percent in each poll -- and at a level matching that of the immensely popular Republican, Ronald Reagan, when he began his second term in 1985.

Furthermore, the polls showed the public generally optimistic about the outlook for the country and his second term, not expecting too much out of him or the Congress by way of achievement and generally content with U.S. economic prosperity.
Clinton, the first Democrat elected to a second term since Franklin Roosevelt 60 years ago, meant to capitalise on those trends with his harmony message.

"He's going to talk to all Americans about everyone coming together to build new communities that really protect Americans, that provide them opportunities, communities in which we can all come together to solve problems," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said in a CNN interview.
"That will only happen, the president will say, if Republicans and Democrats can reeach across their differences, set aside partisan bickering aand really get down to work."

McCurry said the address would also contain a message for the international audience, "a very strong assertion of Americas indispensable role as a force for peace, freedom and democracy throughout the world."
Clinton, notorious for being long-winded, held his first inaugural address to a crisp 14 minutes four years ago and there were indications he was striving for brevity again.

But he could not resist tinkering with his speech to the very last minute. "I think he will probably be scribbling all the way up there (in the ride to Capitol Hill), but that's the way he makes this speech really his own," McCurry said.

Clinton's big day began at a long, tuneful gospel-style church service at church that normally has a predominantly black congregation near the White House, although it was jammed mostly with white, male, middle-aged guests for this occasion. Clinton heard many prayers, gospel songs and chants of "God will heal the land."
The inaugural ceremony was to be followed by a two-hour parade along Pennsylvania Avenue featuring colourul contingents for all over the country and by black-tie balls at night.
